# What pyiceberg's declaration gate costs, catalog by catalog.
# Generated by gate_cost.py. A join over paper 1's stored evidence and
# the two client maps -- no network, and nothing measured here that was
# not measured somewhere else first.

  pyiceberg compares every endpoint against the `endpoints` array of
  GET /v1/config before sending (rest/__init__.py:649). The Rust crate
  has no such check. So for an endpoint a catalog serves without
  declaring, the two clients differ on whether the request is sent at
  all -- and the client that can express fewer operations is the one
  that will try.

  Paper 1's words are used unchanged: `undeclared, works` is an
  endpoint that answered without being named, `DECLARED, FAILS` is the
  other direction.

## Working endpoints, and whether the gate lets the client ask

  catalog                declared  sends   blocked  substituted  of blocked,
                                                                 rust can send
  apache-polaris         36        23      1        0            0
  aws-glue               none      11      0        2            0
  aws-s3tables           none      11      0        2            0
  databricks-unity       18        15      0        0            0
  google-lakehouse       15        14      0        0            0
  microsoft-onelake      13        8       0        0            0
  snowflake-horizon      23        14      1        0            0

  declared    size of the catalog's `endpoints` array. `none` means the
              array was absent, and the client falls back to twelve
              namespace and table endpoints -- no HEADs, no credentials,
              no scan planning, and no views unless the caller asks.
  sends       working endpoints the gate lets through.
  blocked     working endpoints the client refuses to call, or answers
              with an empty list without calling.
  substituted working endpoints answered by a different request.

## The size of it

  Across the seven catalogs the gate blocks 2 working endpoint(s) in
  total, all of them load_credentials, and substitutes a different
  request for 4 more. 3 of the seven are untouched by it. In 0 of the
  blocked cases the Rust crate could have sent the request, so on this
  evidence the gate does not move the comparison between the two
  clients.

  The mechanism is real and the cost is small, which is two separate
  statements and both belong in the paper. What makes the cost small
  here is that the endpoints catalogs underclaim are mostly ones
  neither client can use: the one endpoint blocked on two catalogs is
  loadCredentials, which the Rust crate has no method for at all.

                                 works on the wire, answered by another request

      head_table                 HEAD /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}
                                 works on the wire, answered by another request

  ### aws-s3tables   (no endpoints array; client falls back to the twelve defaults, paper 1 run 2026-09-03T21:32:09Z)

      head_namespace             HEAD /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}
                                 works on the wire, answered by another request

      head_table                 HEAD /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}
                                 works on the wire, answered by another request

  ### databricks-unity   (18 endpoints declared, paper 1 run 2026-09-03T21:32:58Z)

      nothing blocked: every working endpoint is declared.

      The gate is not a correctness filter, only a filter on underclaims.
      databricks-unity: plan_table_scan, update_namespace_props --
      declared and does not work, so the client sends the request and gets
      the catalog's error, exactly as the Rust crate would.

  ### google-lakehouse   (15 endpoints declared, paper 1 run 2026-09-03T21:31:59Z)

      nothing blocked: every working endpoint is declared.

      The gate is not a correctness filter, only a filter on underclaims.
      google-lakehouse: load_credentials -- declared and does not work, so
      the client sends the request and gets the catalog's error, exactly
      as the Rust crate would.

  ### microsoft-onelake   (13 endpoints declared, paper 1 run 2026-09-03T21:32:02Z)

      nothing blocked: every working endpoint is declared.

      The gate is not a correctness filter, only a filter on underclaims.
      microsoft-onelake: commit_table, create_namespace, create_table,
      rename_table -- declared and does not work, so the client sends the
      request and gets the catalog's error, exactly as the Rust crate
      would.

  ### snowflake-horizon   (23 endpoints declared, paper 1 run 2026-09-03T21:32:34Z)

      load_credentials           GET /v1/{prefix}/namespaces/{namespace}/tables/{table}/credentials
                                 works on the wire, client refuses
                                 rust: cannot express it either (absent)

      The gate is not a correctness filter, only a filter on underclaims.
      snowflake-horizon: commit_transaction, create_view, list_views,
      update_namespace_props -- declared and does not work, so the client
      sends the request and gets the catalog's error, exactly as the Rust
      crate would.

## What is measured here and what is modelled

  apache-polaris is measured: both clients have been run against it,
  and evidence/pyiceberg-run-apache-polaris.json records the two cells
  the client refused.

  The other six are modelled. The `endpoints` array is paper 1's, read
  from a stored /v1/config response; what the client does with it is
  read from the client's source. Neither client has been run against
  those catalogs, so every row for them is a prediction that a vendor
  run can falsify -- which is the point of writing it down first.

  Paper 1's own caveats carry over unchanged: three of the seven were
  measured on trial accounts, managed catalogs expose no version, and
  each run is one region at one moment.
